A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WildSAT. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original satellite classification, bird encounter-rate prediction, retrieval and ablation results, including Tables 1–4 and supplementary experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds segmentation, multispectral evaluation and quantitative zero-shot classification results.

M1.justification: The WildSAT contrastive objectives, SINR/GritLM encoders, projection heads and fine-tuning rules remain unchanged. v2 adds a task-specific segmentation adaptation: a trainable U-Net-style convolutional decoder attached to a frozen ResNet50 encoder, extending the linear-head downstream procedure in v1 (Section 5 and Appendix C.1).

E1.justification: v2 adds Cashew1k plantation segmentation in Benin and SAcrop3k crop segmentation in South Africa, substantially extending evaluation beyond image classification and bird encounter rates. It also evaluates zero-shot classification on selected EuroSAT and So2Sat20k classes, previously evaluated through trained linear probes.

E2.justification: RemoteCLIP joins the existing CLIP, TaxaBind and GRAFT classification comparison in v2 Tables 2 and A3, and participates in the new zero-shot comparison in Table A5. The previously evaluated comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New segmentation experiments train U-Net-style decoders with frozen encoders and report IoU and pixel accuracy. v2 also adds zero-shot classwise F1 evaluation and multispectral runs using available bands, zero-filling only unavailable bands instead of all non-RGB bands. These are additional protocols; the original RGB classification experiments and WildSAT training budget remain.

E4.justification: The component, location-encoder and PEFT ablations and So2Sat20k confusion matrices are retained unchanged. v2 adds focused multispectral checks, a diagnostic comparison of zero-shot performance on natural versus anthropogenic classes, and segmentation case studies highlighting corrected crop predictions (Tables A4–A5 and Figure A3).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The connecting lines in v2 Figure 3 represent base-to-WildSAT performance changes, not uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative results. Examples include SatlasNet Cashew1k IoU of 55.2%/71.0% for base/+WildSAT, multispectral Prithvi-100M So2Sat20k accuracy of 28.7%/50.1%, and zero-shot WildSAT F1 of 87.4 on SeaLake versus 0.4 on Highway. These are newly reported evaluations, not gains over v1 under identical conditions. The original classification, bird-encounter and ablation tables retain their values.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and three contrastive-loss equations are equivalent across versions. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that wildlife observations improve and complement satellite representations, benefit pretrained models, outperform competing cross-modal approaches and enable text-based retrieval. The conclusion is retained. Segmentation and multispectral experiments broaden support for the existing general-applicability claim rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies poor zero-shot performance on anthropogenic classes and suggests combining wildlife and anthropogenic supervision. It also discusses African segmentation transfer and relates larger US bird-prediction gains to training geography. Conversely, it removes v1's polar-coverage and endangered-species caveats. The PEFT and location-encoder interpretations promoted into the main text already appeared in v1's appendix.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository pointer and discloses negative sampling, species/location text matching, use of supplied dataset splits, and average training time of eight hours on two NVIDIA L40S GPUs. It documents missing-band handling for the new multispectral experiments. The endangered-species exclusion/location-noise disclosure is removed, without establishing that the underlying processing changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of WikiSatNet as a close predecessor, EcoWikiRS and RemoteCLIP, explicitly credits TaxaBind's earlier combination of species locations and satellite imagery, and adds references supporting segmentation. This sharpens the distinction between wildlife and anthropogenic supervision while retaining the original research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction and related work, moves Dataset from Section 3.2 into a standalone Section 4, and summarizes existing appendix interpretations in the main text. The method exposition, conclusion and much supplementary prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v1's main classification Table 1 moves to v2 Table A1, while a new multipanel Figure 3 visualizes those results. v2 adds segmentation, multispectral and zero-shot tables plus segmentation visualizations, and reduces the main retrieval image grid. These changes substantially reorganize the presentation of evidence beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's broad representation-learning claims. Frozen-encoder segmentation tests establish transfer to dense prediction, multispectral experiments address the RGB-only restriction on compatible pretrained models, and quantitative zero-shot results reveal concrete applicability limits absent from v1's qualitative retrieval examples. Added implementation and access information also helps reproducibility. Removing the polar-coverage and endangered-species caveats reduces transparency, but this limited loss is outweighed by the stronger and better-qualified empirical evidence.
